# Report: Newton & Miah, *Learning Styles in UK Higher Education* (survey study)

## 1. The question, frozen

The paper answers several questions. The one its opening and aims make central is: **do academics in UK Higher Education believe in Learning Styles, and do they actually use them — and how do the two compare with each other and with techniques that have evidence behind them?**

Range: UK HE staff reached indirectly through eight institutions, one online form open two months, voluntary, anonymous, self-report; 161 started, 114 finished. What is asked: mostly *what can we tell from what we see* (estimated from self-reports). A second question is bolted on at the end – *why does the myth persist, and how should we address it?* – which is a *what produces it* question and is not answered by counting answers. I keep the first frozen and flag the second where it matters.

## 2. The explanation in parts

The study's parts, in its own words: a survey whose title never says "Learning Styles", sent indirectly to avoid a self-selected, worked-up pool; a convenience sample (N unknown at the sending end); a list of five methods, four evidence-based, ranked for effectiveness; a self-report of which methods were used in the last 12 months (33% Learning Styles); specific instruments (Honey & Mumford 18.5%, Kolb 14.5%, VARK 12.9%, Felder 1.6%); the Dekker sentence (58% agree); "I try to organize my teaching to accommodate different student Learning Styles" (64%); a paragraph of evidence read mid-form; a harms list drawn from the debunking literature, mixed with reasons to keep using; a before/after pair; a split of the 31.6% who still plan to use against the 43.9% who don't; a Spearman test on reading the literature; free-text themes; and four offered explanations – conflation with "variety of methods", social desirability, the backfire effect, and awareness-raises-use.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral title, indirect distribution | Held if | Removing it breaks the stated job (an unbiassed pool). But the job is in doubt: the counterfactual was never run, so what it actually did to responses is unmeasured. |
| Convenience sample, unknown denominator | Fixed | The authors state it and can't test it; it limits every percentage. |
| Five-method list and ranking | Held | The dropout data do the work: most non-completers stopped right after this question. That is a measured reading, not an assertion. |
| The 33% "used Learning Styles" figure | Loose | Swap the definition of "use" (self-defined matching vs. ever giving a questionnaire) and the number moves. The two 33%s are two different questions landing together by luck, not two routes to one job. |
| "Microteaching 12%" | Loose | The paper itself says the word may not be understood. A naming artefact, not a finding about practice. |
| Dekker sentence vs "I try to organize…" (58% / 64%) | Two routes | Either wording carries "most of them say they believe". What is held is *a majority*; the exact figure is not. |
| Evidence paragraph read mid-form | Held if | It only does work paired with the before/after intention question; that pair is the whole "we didn't just push them" claim. |
| Before/after intention shift | Held | Remove it and "completing the form moved them" has no support anywhere. |
| Split of persisters vs non-persisters | Built, then fitted | Designed as description, but run post hoc at a reviewer's request; it says who, not why. |
| Spearman test on literature reading | Idle | Drop it and nothing in the report changes: no power stated, no discussion, no rival ruled out. |
| Harms list drawn from prior papers | Fitted | Tuned on the same sources whose conclusion the paper then recommends. |
| Free-text themes (48 comments) | Held if | Themes are real, but two authors reading and agreeing on counts is a weak hold, and the "conflation" reading is theirs, not the participants'. |
| Awareness → use ("it seems reasonable to infer") | Asserted | One-off self-reports; the arrow could run the other way. Never poked. |
| Social desirability, backfire effect | Catch-alls | Both absorb any result. No gauge given. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Belief at 58% is read as a decline (93→76→64→58). Had it been 93% the paper would still have a reading ("belief persists"); had it been 15% ("debunking works"). The trend sentence covers any outcome – and it borrows three studies with different countries, populations and instruments, which the paper concedes.

**Reverse.** "Participants use techniques they consider effective, so raising awareness raises use." The same one page of self-report supports the reverse: people rate as effective what they already do. "It seems reasonable to infer" is the tell.

**Answer in the starting points.** 90% agree the theory is conceptually flawed, and the recommendation is – attack the conceptual flaw. The agreement was expected by the authors' own admission, because participants had just been told. What survives is the *ordering* among harms under this set-up, not the levels.

**Pull.** "Reassuring" and "pessimistic" readings of the same 33% sit in one discussion with nothing to decide between them. "Raise awareness of effective methods" pulls against "debunking may backfire".

**Add a job.** If non-use rested on not understanding, the 31.6% who still plan to use should be the ones who say the form didn't help. Instead 64% say it did. The understanding story needs a patch ("social desirability"), and that patch can explain anything – including the opposite.

**Change list.** Covered: sector, country, year, before/after the evidence, within-sample groups. Left out openly: whether people actually match teaching to styles, and the views of the 47 who quit – both stated. Left out quietly: any student outcome whatsoever. Nothing here measures learning; the whole claim is about what academics say.

**Where the parts came from.** Fitted: harms list, five-method set, Dekker sentence, dropout benchmark. Built: the before/after design. Asserted: the causal arrow, the backfire claim.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

One cut and one job. (1) Drop the Spearman test and the "microteaching" row, or replace the word with "peer observation of teaching" and re-ask – both are doing nothing or doing harm. (2) Add one job: show that the neutral title changed who answered. Half of that poke is already runnable – send the same form titled "Learning Styles" to a matched group. If the numbers move, the anti-bias part is held; if not, it is decoration.

## 6. What this shows and does not

Loose is not wrong: the 58% may be exactly right. This only says which parts are pinned and which could be swapped without the study noticing. It cannot say whether the reading of the evidence about Learning Styles is correct – that rests on other work.

## 7. One next step

Before collecting more, write down what would count as the survey having gone wrong, then run the title swap on one institution and report both numbers side by side.

Question frozen: The paper answers several questions. The one its opening/title makes central: Do UK HE academics believe in Learning Styles, and do they use them — and how do the two compare with each other and with evidence-based methods? Kind of question: mostly "what can we tell from what we see" (a backward/measurement question, from self-reports) with a bolted-on "what produces it" (why the myth persists) and a purpose question (how best to address it).

Range: UK HE academics reached indirectly through 8 institutions, ~10 min online survey, over 2 months; self-report; N=114 completers.

Jobs, each as a contrast:
- Given: belief majority vs. the 93% schoolteacher figure — why lower? And why still a majority given no evidence?
- Given: use lower than belief, and lower than evidence-based methods.
- Given: intention drops after evidence is shown, but ~a third still persist.
- Given (harms): which proposed harm is most compelling, and not the others.
- Added (mine): why 90% call the theory conceptually flawed while a third still use it — that's the sharpest joint.
- Added: why no link between reading the literature and belief.

Parts (owner's words): neutral title/indirect distribution; convenience sample N=161/114; list of 5 methods + ranking by efficacy; specific instruments (VARK, Kolb, Felder, H&M); Dekker statement; "I try to organize my teaching…"; the evidence paragraph read mid-survey; harms list from the debunking literature, interspersed with reasons to use; pre/post intention comparison; subgroup split of persisters vs non-persisters; Spearman correlation; free-text themes; the discussion's explanations (variety-of-methods conflation, social desirability, backfire effect, awareness→use causality).

Change list: covered — population (schoolteachers vs HE, UK vs US), time (2012→2016 trend), point in survey (before vs after evidence), sub-groups within the sample (persisters vs non). Left out, not stated up front: observed teaching rather than reported; the fate of the 47 non-completers' views; what the survey intro did to the pool (asserted, never measured); student outcomes — no outcome at all; discipline/age splits (stated as a limit; fine); whether the persisters match instruction to style (stated as a limit — good).

Tests:
Remove:
- Remove the pre/post pair → the "completing it helped / they won't continue" claim loses its only two points. Held by that job.
- Remove the Dekker sentence → comparisons with 2012/2014 go; belief-vs-use gap survives.
- Remove the sector-level subgroup split → "who persists" unanswered.
- Remove the neutral title/indirect distribution → the anti-bias argument goes, but no measured difference (they never ran the counterfactual) → held if.
- Remove the Spearman correlation → nothing else in the report changes; idle.
- Remove pairs: the "evidence presented mid-survey" + "neutral framing" together carry the whole "we didn't push them" claim.

Swap:
- Swap the Dekker wording ("individuals learn better when...") for "I try to organize my teaching to accommodate different student Learning Styles" → 58% vs 64%. Both work for "a majority believe". So the exact 58% is loose; what's held is a majority. Rename: "a majority of these academics say they believe" — measurement of belief, not belief itself.
- Swap formative assessment/peer teaching out of the five methods → "use is lower than evidence-based methods" depends on the set. Microteaching at 12%: the paper itself says participants may not know what the word means → the low number may be a naming artefact. So the ordering claim is held by the list; the part "microteaching" is loose (a label).
- Swap "used Learning Styles in the last 12 months" definition → 33% moves; the two 33%s (used as a method; ever gave a questionnaire) agreeing is a nice coincidence but they're two different asks.

Flip the outcome:
- Belief 58% = "declining trend, reassuring". Had it been 93%, they'd have said belief persists; had it been 15%, they'd have said debunking works. The trend sentence covers any point → loose, and it's borrowed from three other studies with different populations and instruments (paper concedes).
- If use were *higher* than evidence-based methods, would the paper have a reading? "The pessimistic interpretation" is already available, so plausibly yes — both readings are on the table in the same discussion. That's the pull.

Reverse:
- "participants use techniques which they consider effective... raise awareness → use will increase." Same one-off self-reports support the arrow either way (rate as effective what you already use). They say "it seems reasonable to infer": that's the tell. Asserted, direction not poked. Held-if at best.

Poke (both halves):
- Change the survey title to name Learning Styles → explanation says response pool shifts (they designed for this) and belief/use answers change. That half is testable and wasn't run. The half that should not matter: e.g. the length of the survey intro. So the neutral-title part is held if.
- Change the opening ranking question → they did observe dropout at that question, so the claim "the ranking question was the hard bit" is held by an internal reading, not asserted. Nice.
- Change only how the number is read — e.g. count "neither agree nor disagree" as disagreement → the 58% stays a measurement of the report; the belief itself does not move. Keep the same part.

Add a job:
- Take the 31.6% who still plan to use it. If the explanation is "they hadn't understood the evidence", they should have said the questionnaire didn't help them. 64% said it did help them understand. That's a job the understanding story fails without a patch. The patch: "social desirability" (they said "helped" to please the authors) — that patch also absorbs "they plan to stop", so it can swallow anything; it needs a gauge: something they could measure that would show it, e.g. whether persisters show the same shift as the rest.

Catch-alls: "social desirability bias" and the "backfire effect" — both can absorb any result; no gauge offered in this data. The persister profile (94% already said they accommodated styles; 89% said experience shows benefit) is a real finding and it points to a much simpler reading: they say what they already do. That's a rival the paper mentions only briefly.

Answer in the starting points: "the theory is conceptually flawed" — the harm list was built by the authors from the same debunking papers whose conclusion (attack the conceptual flaw) they then recommend. Agreement was expected (they say so). So the top ranking is held by a job in doubt: what it does show is the *ordering* among the harms, given the setup. Held if.

Pull: "reassuring" vs "pessimistic" readings of 33% — both in the same discussion, nothing decided. Also "raise awareness of effective methods" pulls against "debunking may backfire".

Where each part came from: Fitted — the harms list (built from prior papers); the five-method comparison set (from earlier work); the Dekker sentence (borrowed for comparability); the 30% dropout benchmark; the post hoc subgroup split (fitted at a reviewer's request). Built — the pre/post design; the decision to hide the term "Learning Styles" (commits to a definite prediction about bias, never checked: "built but untested" — hmm, mark held-if); the definition of "use". Asserted — awareness→use causality; backfire relevance.
